listing_view.reasoning: Demand is weak — the book was only ~0.86x subscribed with one day to go, and the underlying trend (revenue down 24% in the latest year, PAT CAGR −14.2%, RoE down to 7.6%) gives little reason for buyers to chase it. With this operating profile and no visible anchor or GMP support, a weak or discounted listing looks more likely than a pop.

longterm_view.reasoning: Reported profits have not arrived as cash in the last two years (operating cash flow of −₹1,970m and −₹3,186m), and against that single strong cash year sits a collapsing top line, falling returns on capital (RoCE 20.4% → 10.6%), and receivables stretching from 35 to 137 days. A business shrinking, earning lower returns, and collecting cash slower is deteriorating on every axis that matters over years.

governance.reasoning: The company, a SEBI-registered Investment Adviser, has received a SEBI show cause notice and was fined ₹4 lakh by SEBI [litigation, page 610][litigation, page 608], with disclosure also covering disciplinary action against promoters [litigation, page 609]. The penalty itself is trivial in size, but a regulator-on-the-record history in a financial-services business is a flag, not noise.

key_risks.risk: Profit is not converting to cash
key_risks.why_it_matters: Two straight years of sharply negative operating cash flow against positive PAT means the earnings quality is questionable and the book may be sustaining itself on credit extended to customers.
Collection period stretched from 35 to 137 days in two years — the latest year's accounting profit is largely sitting unpaid with customers.
Latest-year revenue fell 24% and RoCE halved to 10.6%, so the company is asking for IPO money while its economics are moving the wrong way.
A SEBI penalty and show cause notice against a SEBI-registered investment adviser signals compliance risk in exactly the licence the business depends on.
At ~0.86x subscription near the close the issue's pricing is being carried by the seller's chosen band, not demonstrated buyer demand.

answers.question: where did the money go — receivables, inventory, or both?
answers.answer: Receivables, clearly. Collection days rose from 35.3 to 137.2 over two years, which matches the negative operating cash flow in the two most recent years — the cash is going out as credit to customers, faster than it comes back. There is no inventory figure in what I was given, so I cannot apportion anything to inventory; but the receivable deterioration alone is large enough to explain the cash drain.

answers.question: who are the customers, and is any of it disputed?
answers.answer: not answerable from what I was given — no customer names, concentration data, or disputed-receivable disclosure appears in the extracts. The only related signal is that disclosures reference a related party ('Analytics and Advisory Private Limited') and collateral kept against bank guarantees, but that does not identify the customer base or disputes.

answer.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that the 137-day receivables are from blue-chip, contractually secured counterparties (e.g., government or exchange-settled flows) with post-year-end collections, plus disclosure that the IPO proceeds fund identifiable high-return deployment rather than filling the working-capital hole. A basis-for-price chapter showing the valuation is modest against peers would also matter — its absence currently leaves the pricing untestable.
